title: The Room Without a Name: Berlin, the Healthy Lung, and the Work That Passed Hand to Hand
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Sewing Room and the Healthy Lung

stops.name: Berlin, the birth into poverty
stops.date_confidence: attested; German and English Wikipedia agree on the day. The city is all the sources give: no district, no street, no parish record was reachable, and the coordinate is the generic Berlin centre.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of June a daughter is born to a poor Berlin family, and the sources that will one day trace a whole century of body-work back to her cannot name the street. No district, no house, no register reaches this file. What is recorded is the poverty: she will finance her own education out of factory wages, domestic service, and sewing taken in at home. The city she is born into is the capital of a new empire that is building gymnastic halls in every quarter and teaching drill to schoolchildren. She will spend seventy-five years inside it and, so far as any reachable source says, never leave.
suggested_refs: Berlin civil registration for June 1885, not located in this run

stops.name: Berlin, the factory, the service, the needle
stops.date_confidence: undated; German Wikipedia gives the three trades for her childhood and youth without a single year. 1900 is a placement inside that period, not an attestation.
stops.campa: Through her girlhood and youth she pays for herself. German Wikipedia gives three trades and not a single year for any of them. No employer is named, no workshop is located, no wage is recorded. The hands that will later teach thousands of people to notice what their own hands are doing learn first at a machine, at another family's stove, and at a needle. The atlas can pin none of it. The sources record a condition where an address would go, and this stop stands on the generic city coordinate.
suggested_refs: Berlin trade and domestic service records for the 1890s, not consulted

stops.name: Berlin, the books of the furniture workshop
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; German Wikipedia gives 1906 and names no firm, so the coordinate remains the generic city centre.
stops.campa: From this year she keeps the books of a Moebeltischlerei, a furniture carpentry business. It is the first employment the sources date, and the last ordinary one. She is twenty-one, sitting at a ledger in a workshop full of men planing wood, and the whole apparatus of her later teaching is fifteen years off. The same autumn, in New York, a German gymnastics teacher named Hedwig Kallmeyer enrolls at Genevieve Stebbins's School of Expression in Carnegie Hall. Neither woman knows the other exists, and the method one of them is fetching is the one the other will spend her life rebuilding.
suggested_refs: Berlin trade directories, 1906, for the unnamed Moebeltischlerei

stops.name: New York, Carnegie Hall, the School of Expression
stops.date_confidence: attested; German Wikipedia dates Kallmeyer's arrival to October 1906 and both diplomas to 1907. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the atlas's stebbins.journey.json.
stops.campa: In Carnegie Music Hall, Genevieve Stebbins has run her School of Expression since 1893, teaching the Delsarte system she received through Steele Mackaye and rebuilt into what she calls harmonic gymnastics. Hedwig Kallmeyer arrives from Germany in October and takes both the voice and the gymnastics diplomas within the year. This is not Gindler's journey; she is in Berlin keeping accounts. It is the room where the method that reaches her was assembled, and the atlas already walks it in the Stebbins file.
suggested_refs: Genevieve Stebbins, Dynamic Breathing and Harmonic Gymnastics (1892)
stebbins.journey.json, the School of Expression founded 1893

stops.name: Dittisham, Devon, Stebbins on the Dart
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the atlas's Stebbins file dates her crossing to September 1907 and German Wikipedia puts Kallmeyer beside her at Dittisham in 1907. This run's geography lens proposed 50.3603 / -3.6067; the existing atlas pin is kept so that two travelers in one village stand on one dot.
stops.campa: Stebbins retires from the New York school and crosses to England, to the village of Dittisham on the tidal Dart. Kallmeyer works beside her here before returning to Germany to found a school of her own. A research lens for this run proposed a Dittisham point two kilometres off the one the atlas already uses. The older pin is kept and the discrepancy is printed; nothing here is averaged. Gindler never comes here. The method does, and it arrives in Berlin in another woman's hands four years before she touches it.
suggested_refs: stebbins.journey.json, the crossing to England, September 1907

stops.name: Berlin, the lung that is left alone
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source consulted. [R]: placed at 1909 by inference only, before the attested 1911 Kallmeyer training, on the reasoning that a self-cure treated as founding should precede the training it founded. It could fall anywhere from the 1890s to 1912.
stops.campa: She contracts tuberculosis. Instead of a sanatorium she performs an experiment on herself: she concentrates her breathing into the healthy lung and leaves the diseased one at rest, and she recovers. Every account of her method turns on this episode, and not one of them gives a year. It is the founding illness of a discipline and it floats free of the calendar. What she takes from it is not a technique but a discovery about attention, that a person can observe the inside of her own body accurately enough to change what it does.
stops.quote: Inadequacy dominates us in general and in particular. Daily there are the same, small, endless, infinitely important mishaps.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People', translation of 'Die Gymnastik des Berufsmenschen' (1926), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 27
suggested_refs: Berlin tuberculosis case records, first decade of the century, not located

segments.name: Kallmeyer's School and the First Room

stops.name: Hellerau, the garden city of the reformed body
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Hellerau institution; [R] as a Gindler stop, since no source connects her to it. Coordinate inherited from suzanne_perrottet.journey.json and mary_wigman.journey.json.
stops.campa: Above Dresden, in a garden city built for the purpose, Emile Jaques-Dalcroze opens a Bildungsanstalt where music is taught through the moving body. Suzanne Perrottet teaches there; Mary Wigman arrives as a student in October. The German-speaking world is in the middle of a general conviction that the body has been ruined by the century and can be trained back. Gindler is in Berlin, four hundred kilometres north, about to enter the same conviction by a different door. No source connects her to Hellerau. The two currents run parallel here and never cross.
suggested_refs: The Festspielhaus at Hellerau

stops.name: Berlin, Kallmeyer's school, the American method
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the meeting and the training; the address is not. The Charlottenburg coordinate is an acknowledged placeholder. A flagged contradiction about the school's Berlin dates dissolves once the 1909 founding is used instead of the later Kallmeyer-Lauterbach phase.
stops.campa: She meets Hedwig Kallmeyer and begins training in Harmonische Gymnastik, the system Kallmeyer brought back from Stebbins in New York. Through this room Gindler inherits the Delsarte line without ever crossing an ocean. The school Kallmeyer founded in 1909 is called Kuenstlerische Gymnastik nach G. Stebbins; the name Kallmeyer-Lauterbach belongs to a later phase and does not apply to this year. No address survives, and the coordinate is an approximate Charlottenburg point rather than a located building.
suggested_refs: Hedwig Kallmeyer, Kuenstlerische Gymnastik nach G. Stebbins, Berlin, founded 1909

stops.name: Berlin, the first independent practice
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season; German Wikipedia specifies autumn 1912, so the day is set to the first of October as a convention. No address is recorded.
stops.campa: In the autumn she separates from Kallmeyer and begins teaching on her own. What she teaches is already not what she was taught. The exercises stay, roughly, but the object of the work moves: away from correct positions imposed from outside, toward the student's own capacity to notice. She is twenty-seven, six years out of the bookkeeper's chair. The address of this first practice is not recorded anywhere reachable. The atlas pins it on the generic Berlin coordinate and claims no street.
stops.quote: It is difficult for me to speak about Gymnastik because the aim of my work is not the learning of certain movements, but rather the achievement of concentration.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People' (1926 lecture), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 27, opening line
suggested_refs: Berlin address books, 1912-1913, for the unlocated first studio

stops.name: Monte Verita, Ascona, the hill she never climbs
stops.date_confidence: [R] and a gap marker. The date is Laban's attested arrival on the hill. No source ties Gindler to Ascona in either direction, and this stop records the corpus's silence rather than a movement of the traveler. Coordinate inherited from laban.journey.json and suzanne_perrottet.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the hill above Ascona the vegetarians, anarchists, nudists and dancers of the life-reform colony are already established, and this summer Rudolf von Laban arrives to found the school that will draw Mary Wigman and Suzanne Perrottet up the slope after him. It is the origin of the whole body-culture wing the atlas already walks. Gindler is not mentioned in connection with Monte Verita in any file in the corpus. This pin marks an absence: nobody knows whether her generation's most famous body-reform colony ever touched her.
suggested_refs: laban.journey.json, arrival on the sacred hill

stops.name: Berlin, the first training group
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by German Wikipedia; no month, no venue, no roll of names.
stops.campa: In the third year of the war she gathers the first group of students she is training not as pupils but as teachers. The work begins to reproduce itself. Nothing is written down; there is no curriculum, no manual, no diploma described in any source found. What passes from her to them passes in a room, through attention paid to breathing and standing and the weight of a shoulder, and it will keep passing that way for forty-four years and across three continents without ever being fixed in a book.
stops.quote: We therefore advise our students from the very first lesson that our work must be pursued consciously; it can only be entered into and understood through consciousness.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People' (1926 lecture), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 27
suggested_refs: Sophie Ludwig, Elsa Gindler, von ihrem Leben und Wirken (secondary literature, not opened in this run)

stops.name: Berlin, the Philharmonie, Wigman dances alone
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date and coordinate are inherited from mary_wigman.journey.json. [R] as a Gindler connection: no crossing between the two women is recorded anywhere.
stops.campa: Mary Wigman brings her solo Ausdruckstanz to the Berlin Philharmonie and dances to a nearly empty house. Within a few years the same city will not be able to get enough of the trained, reformed, expressive body: Laban's institute, Wigman's schools, Mensendieck and Bode and Loheland, gymnastic halls in every district. Gindler works this current from its quietest end, in a private room with a handful of people at a time. The two women share a capital and a decade, and no file in the corpus records them ever meeting.
suggested_refs: mary_wigman.journey.json, the Philharmonie nearly empty

stops.name: Hamburg, Contrology and the police
stops.date_confidence: attested for Pilates; coordinate inherited from joseph_pilates.journey.json. [R] as a Gindler connection: the kinship is at the level of a movement, not a meeting.
stops.campa: Joseph Pilates is in Hamburg training the city police and building the apparatus of what he calls Contrology, and the following year Laban's Hamburg dance school takes his exercises up alongside Bess Mensendieck's Koerperkultur. It is the same German medical-gymnastic movement that produced Kallmeyer, and through Kallmeyer produced Gindler. No meeting between Gindler and Pilates is attested anywhere. The kinship is at the level of a whole country deciding at once that the body could be taught and had been neglected.
suggested_refs: joseph_pilates.journey.json, training the police, the Foot Corrector

stops.name: Berlin, Heinrich Jacoby
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by German Wikipedia and the English Jacoby article; the venue of the first meeting is not recorded.
stops.campa: She meets the music pedagogue Heinrich Jacoby, who is arguing that musicality is not a gift given to some and withheld from others but a capacity every human being has and most have lost. She is arguing the same thing about movement. The collaboration that begins here will run thirty-seven years, survive his exile and her bombing, and never acquire a name; the two of them will simply call it the work. Where in Berlin they first met is not recorded in anything this run could reach.
suggested_refs: Heinrich Jacoby, Jenseits von musikalisch und unmusikalisch

stops.name: Berlin, the sixty instructors
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives the figure for the mid-1920s without a year; 1925 is the midpoint of that phrase. German Wikipedia gives the number and no roll of names.
stops.campa: By the middle of the decade she has trained roughly sixty gymnastics instructors. The method has stopped being one woman's practice and become a network. They carry it into schools, clinics and private studios across Germany. She writes no textbook for them. What each of them takes away is what her own body learned in the room. The transmission is exact where it works and unrecoverable where it fails. The sources give the figure and not one name attached to it.
stops.quote: The student begins to feel that he is in charge of himself. He suddenly feels that if he wishes he can work on his whole body in the same manner that he worked on his shoulder-girdle.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People' (1926 lecture), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 28
suggested_refs: Registers of the Deutscher Gymnastik-Bund, 1925-1933, not located

stops.name: Berlin, the Deutscher Gymnastik-Bund
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; contradiction printed and not resolved, since German Wikipedia's article on the association credits Franz Hilker alone and does not name Gindler, while its article on Gindler makes her co-founder. The founding venue is unrecorded.
stops.campa: With the pedagogue Franz Hilker she co-founds the German Gymnastics Association, an umbrella drawing the previously separate schools of Bode, Medau, Kallmeyer, Laban, Loheland and Mensendieck into one professional body. She will serve as deputy chairwoman until 1933. The sources do not agree about her billing: the encyclopedia's article on Gindler makes her co-founder, while its article on the association credits Hilker alone and never names her. The disagreement stands unresolved here, printed and not adjudicated.
suggested_refs: Franz Hilker's papers on the Deutscher Gymnastikbund, not consulted

stops.name: Berlin, Die Gymnastik des Berufsmenschen
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year. Title corrected: one research lens rendered it 'Gymnastik des arbeitenden Menschen', which is not what German Wikipedia says. The venue is not given and may have been a Gymnastikbund congress outside Berlin.
stops.campa: She delivers a lecture called the gymnastics of the working person, and it becomes the only thing she ever publishes. In it she refuses almost everything the word gymnastics means to her audience: no repetition, no correct position, no instructor's hand moving a limb into place. What she offers instead is concentration, and the proposition that a correction imposed from outside is worth very little. Every English word of hers the twentieth century possesses comes out of this one text.
stops.quote: To this we can only reply that our work is not Gymnastik in the ordinary sense, which certainly does not bring about consciousness: what does is the mind that is present and concentrated on situation.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People' (1926 lecture), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 27
suggested_refs: Elsa Gindler Volume 1 (Sensory Awareness Foundation, 1978)
USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3 No. 1 (2004), pp. 27-30
sources: USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), read as PDF

stops.name: Halensee, the villa of Hertha Feist
stops.date_confidence: attested for Lindenberg's diploma year; coordinate inherited from elsa_lindenberg.journey.json.
stops.campa: In a villa in Halensee, Hertha Feist runs Laban's Berlin outpost, and a scholarship child named Elsa Lindenberg takes her diploma here this year. Lindenberg has Laban's spatial choreology in her legs and will shortly go looking for something else, something smaller and slower and turned inward. The atlas already walks her journey. She is the single body in which the Laban wing and the Gindler wing of this corpus are joined, and she finds the second of them a few streets east.
suggested_refs: elsa_lindenberg.journey.json, the villa of Hertha Feist

stops.name: Berlin, Charlotte Selver comes to the room
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia says only 'during the 1920s'; 1927 is a placement inside that decade. The Kurfuerstenstrasse coordinate is Gindler's best-documented later studio street, and whether the practice was already there in the late 1920s is not established.
stops.campa: Charlotte Selver becomes Gindler's student and also Jacoby's, and stays through the end of the decade and into the next. She is learning a practice with no name, no notation and no literature. In America she will have to invent an English name for it. What she is taught, among other things, is how to stand. The coordinate here is Kurfuerstenstrasse, the street of Gindler's best-documented studio; whether the practice was already at that address in the late 1920s is not established by any source found.
stops.quote: As for standing - real standing - we must feel how we give our weight, pound for pound, onto the earth, and how in doing so the feet become steadily lighter. Here is a paradox: the weightier we become the lighter we become and the quieter we become.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People' (1926 lecture), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 30. The em-dashed form is the printed text; a research lens rendered it with commas.
suggested_refs: Charlotte Selver Foundation archive, not consulted

stops.name: Berlin, Laban brings the Institute to the capital
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and coordinate inherited from laban.journey.json. [R] as a Gindler connection: adjacency only.
stops.campa: Rudolf von Laban moves his Choreographisches Institut from Wuerzburg to Berlin in October. The capital now holds, within a few kilometres of each other, the largest dance-notation project in Europe and a woman teaching four people at a time to feel the weight of their own shoulders. Weimar Berlin's obsession with the reformed body runs through both. No source records Laban and Gindler in the same room, and this stop asserts adjacency and nothing more. The pin is the one the atlas already uses for the Institute.
suggested_refs: laban.journey.json, the Institute moves to the capital

stops.name: Berlin, the quiet room of Elsa Gindler
stops.date_confidence: the Lindenberg file dates the study loosely across roughly 1927 to 1933; 1928 is a placement inside that range. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from elsa_lindenberg.journey.json.
stops.campa: Lindenberg becomes Gindler's student, and the atlas has already recorded the room from her side: a quiet place where nothing is written down and the work passes hand to hand like a rite. She will hold both disciplines at once, Laban's architecture of space and Gindler's micro-attention to a single joint. Within five years she will carry the second of them out of Germany in her body, which is the only container it has. Her file dates the study loosely, across the last Weimar years, and gives no month.
suggested_refs: Geuter, Heller and Weaver, 'Elsa Gindler and her influence on Wilhelm Reich', Body, Movement and Dance in Psychotherapy 5:1 (2010)
elsa_lindenberg.journey.json

stops.name: Berlin, Carola Speads and Lily Ehrenfried
stops.date_confidence: no year of entry is recorded for either woman; 1930 is a placement inside the decade. Both are now [A] rather than [R]: German Wikipedia names Speads in its own Gindler student list, and the German Ehrenfried article states her study with Gindler outright.
stops.campa: Two more students pass through the room, and both will teach elsewhere. Carola Speads will take the work to New York and call it Physical Re-Education; Lily Ehrenfried will take it to Paris and build Gymnastique Holistique out of it. Both are named independently by the German and the English encyclopedias, which is more corroboration than most of the roster gets. Neither year of entry is recorded. The date here places them inside the decade and asserts nothing about either woman.
stops.quote: The first stumbling block is when I answer that I would not think of getting rid of someone else's stomach; the person would have to do that for himself.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People' (1926 lecture), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 28
suggested_refs: Lily Ehrenfried, De l'education du corps a l'equilibre de l'esprit
Carola Speads, Ways to Better Breathing

stops.name: Berlin, Laura Perls learns the body
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by German Wikipedia on Lore Perls. Upgraded from a research lens's [R]: this is not traditional attribution. The English Laura Perls page omits Gindler, which is a gap on that page rather than a contradiction.
stops.campa: Lore Perls, who will be Laura Perls in America, begins practising and studying sensitive body and movement work with Gindler this year. She and Fritz Perls are living in Berlin and will flee in 1933; the Gestalt therapy they build afterwards in South Africa and New York carries this room inside it. The English page on Laura Perls omits Gindler entirely, and the German page on Lore Perls dates the study exactly. An omission on one page is a gap, not a refutation of the other.
stops.quote: As long as they remain just words, they create mischief; as soon as they are imbued with experience they become great mediators of life.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People' (1926 lecture), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 28, on the words breathing, relaxation, tension
suggested_refs: Laura Perls, Living at the Boundary

stops.name: Berlin, deputy chair until the seizure
stops.date_confidence: the term runs from roughly 1925 to 1933; 1932 marks the last full year rather than an event. German Wikipedia gives the office and the end point and no dates in between.
stops.campa: She has been deputy chairwoman of the German Gymnastics Association since its founding, and this is the last full year of it. In January of the next year the regime takes power and the professional bodies of the republic are dissolved or absorbed into the new order. She holds no office after this. What she keeps is a private practice, a list of students, and a method that exists nowhere except in the people who have it. That is the only form of it the next twelve years cannot confiscate.
suggested_refs: Records of the Deutscher Gymnastik-Bund up to its Gleichschaltung, not located

stops.name: Charlottenburg, the Staedtische Oper casts Lindenberg out
stops.date_confidence: the civil service law is dated exactly; the Lindenberg file places her expulsion under it. Coordinate inherited from elsa_lindenberg.journey.json.
stops.campa: The civil service law of the seventh of April strips Jewish and politically suspect employees from state institutions, and Elsa Lindenberg is put out of the corps de ballet of the Staedtische Oper. The Berlin that trained her closes. She will go north within months, to Copenhagen and then Oslo, carrying Laban in her legs and Gindler in her attention. The route from Berlin to Scandinavia that the atlas already narrates in her file begins at this door, and the method leaves the country with her.
suggested_refs: elsa_lindenberg.journey.json, cast out of the Opera

stops.name: Zurich, Jacoby forbidden to work
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month is given, and the June date is a convention. His residency is not regularised until 1947.
stops.campa: Heinrich Jacoby is compelled to leave Germany and settles in Switzerland, where for years he is officially barred from working or publishing and lives on private support. The collaboration does not stop; it becomes correspondence and, later, holiday courses across a border. Gindler stays in Berlin. No record was found of her ever visiting him here, or of her leaving Germany at all, in the twelve years of the regime or in the sixteen years after it. His residency is not put right until 1947.
suggested_refs: Swiss alien police files on Heinrich Jacoby, 1933-1947, not consulted

stops.name: Copenhagen, the somatic knowledge in the house
stops.date_confidence: the Lindenberg file dates the Copenhagen household to 1933-1934 without a month; coordinate inherited from elsa_lindenberg.journey.json.
stops.campa: Lindenberg reaches Copenhagen and moves into the exile household of Wilhelm Reich, and her file states the transaction plainly: trained by Laban and Gindler, she is the somatic knowledge in the house. Reich is at work on what will become vegetotherapy, a psychoanalysis conducted through the breathing and the musculature. Gindler, who never met him and is teaching in Berlin under the regime he fled, is one of its two stated parents. The transmission is a dancer's body walking north.
suggested_refs: Geuter, Heller and Weaver, 'Elsa Gindler and her influence on Wilhelm Reich' (2010)
reich.journey.json

stops.name: Berlin, the courses that hide people
stops.date_confidence: the practice is attested for the whole 1933-1945 period without a single dated incident; 1935 is a placement inside it. No name, no address, no case is documented in anything reachable.
stops.campa: She rejects the regime and does not emigrate, and she uses the ordinary business of gymnastics instruction as cover. Persecuted people, Jewish students among them, are helped through her practice. That is the whole of what two encyclopedias will say. Not one name, not one incident, not one address is documented in anything this run could reach. The general fact is attested and the particulars are a gap. This file prints both and furnishes no scene it cannot source.
stops.quote: Generally speaking, in all of this, the most essential things we have to keep in mind are: that any correction made from without is of little value, and that each of us must try to gain understanding for the special nature of our own constitution in order to learn how to take care of ourselves.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Gindler, 'Gymnastik for Busy People' (1926 lecture), USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 30, closing paragraph
suggested_refs: Berlin Gedenkstaette Deutscher Widerstand files, not searched in this run

stops.name: New York, Charlotte Selver lands
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the English and German Selver articles; no month is given.
stops.campa: Selver leaves Germany and arrives in New York. Contact with Gindler and Jacoby lapses and will not resume for more than a decade. She carries a practice with no name into a country that has no word for it, and she will have to build both a vocabulary and an audience before anyone can be taught anything. Everything American somatics eventually receives from Berlin comes through this crossing, carried in the memory of one person's attention and in no document at all.
suggested_refs: Charlotte Selver, Waking Up: The Work of Charlotte Selver

stops.name: Zurich, the holiday courses
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1939 as the state of the collaboration; German Wikipedia dates no individual course. The Zurich pin stands for Switzerland generally, and the Italian venues are unlocated.
stops.campa: By this year the joint work with Jacoby survives only as courses held on holiday, in Switzerland and in Italy, because he cannot work openly in Germany and she will not leave it. Two teachers with one method arrange to be in the same country for a few weeks at a time. In September the arrangement ends. The sources do not say whether Gindler attended these courses herself or whether the phrase describes Jacoby's teaching alone. Both readings stay open here.
suggested_refs: Jacoby-Gindler course notes, 1930s, held by the foundation and not reachable in this run

stops.name: Kurfuerstenstrasse, the practice burns
stops.date_confidence: no exact date. German Wikipedia says 'kurz vor Ende des Zweiten Weltkriegs', so 1944 or 1945, and November 1944 is a midpoint. Street corrected from a research lens's Kurfuerstendamm reading, which names a different Berlin street two kilometres away. Two lenses give the street two different coordinates, 52.5023 / 13.3597 and 52.5027 / 13.3389; the first is used and the disagreement stands.
stops.campa: Shortly before the end of the war, bombs destroy her practice on the Kurfuerstenstrasse and most of the documentation of her work burns with it. Forty years of teaching leave one published lecture. A research lens for this run placed the destruction on the Kurfuerstendamm in 1943; the German source names the Kurfuerstenstrasse and says only that it happened shortly before the end. Two streets, two kilometres apart, and no house number exists on either of them in any source found.
stops.quote: This article, written early in her work, is the only piece she published and all that was not burned when her studio was destroyed in the final months of World War II.
stops.quote_source: Editorial abstract preceding Gindler's essay, USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), p. 27. These are the journal editors' words, not Gindler's.
suggested_refs: Berlin bomb-damage maps for Tiergarten and Schoeneberg, 1944-1945
sources: USA Body Psychotherapy Journal Vol. 3/4 (2004/2005), read as PDF

stops.name: New York, the name Gindler never gave
stops.date_confidence: no year is given in any source for the coinage. 1945 is an ordering device only, placed between Selver's 1938 arrival and her 1963 Esalen teaching.
stops.campa: Neither Gindler nor Jacoby ever gave the joint work a formal name in their working lives. In America, Selver needs one, and coins Sensory Awareness. The thing that had been simply the work in a Berlin room becomes a discipline with a title, a title its originator will never use. No source found gives the year of the coinage. The date on this stop orders the sequence and claims nothing. In Germany the work still goes unnamed, and Gindler is still teaching under it.

stops.name: Berlin-Dahlem, the room begun again

stops.campa: After the war she founds a new teaching space in Berlin-Dahlem, in the American sector, and works there until she dies. She is sixty-one. The archive is ash, the association is gone, the students are scattered across three continents or dead, and she starts a room again. What she teaches in it is what she taught in 1912, because there was never anything in it to lose but paper. The German source gives no year and no street, and the coordinate marks the centre of the district. No building is identified.
stops.quote: For us relaxation is that condition in which we have the greatest capacity of reacting. It is a stillness within us, a readiness to respond appropriately to any stimulus.

stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by German and English Wikipedia. The burial place is a gap: no cemetery, plot or stone is named in either encyclopedia, and a findagrave lookup returned HTTP 403.
stops.campa: She dies on the eighth of January, seventy-five years old, in the city she was born in and appears never to have left. No source consulted names a cemetery, a plot, or a stone; the German and English encyclopedias are both silent, and a grave lookup returned an access error. The woman whose entire method consisted of attention paid to a living body leaves no located remains and one published essay. What she leaves instead is in Oslo, Paris, New York and Zurich, walking around inside other people.

stops.campa: Heinrich Jacoby dies in Zurich three years after Gindler, having spent most of his forty years of collaboration with her separated from her by a border. A Jacoby-Gindler foundation and a Swiss association carry the pedagogy forward from here; the foundation's own site did not resolve on this run, so nothing is asserted about what it does now. The work still has no name of its own in Germany. In California it is Sensory Awareness, in Paris Gymnastique Holistique, and in Oslo it is simply what Elsa taught.
